course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
title: Linear Transformations and Standard Matrices
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
sessionGoal: Students should be able to build standard matrices, compute transformations, and connect one-to-one/onto with pivots and matrix shape.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with: a linear transformation is controlled by what it does to basis vectors.
Remind students that columns are images of basis vectors.
Do Problem 2 to connect transformations with kernel/range.
Do Problem 3 to show how to use nonstandard input vectors.
sayThisFirst: A linear transformation is a function that respects adding and scaling.
The standard matrix is built from where the standard basis vectors go.
The columns of the matrix are \(T(e_1)\), \(T(e_2)\), and so on.
Kernel means inputs that go to zero.
Range means outputs the transformation can hit.
boardPlan: Draw a small before/after picture: input vector goes in, output vector comes out.
Problem 1: build a 2 by 2 matrix from \(T(e_1)\), \(T(e_2)\).
Problem 2: find kernel and range for a map from \(\mathbb{R}^3\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
Problem 3: use linearity when the given vectors are not \(e_1\) and \(e_2\).

keyFormulas.name: Standard matrix
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: The columns are where the standard basis vectors land.

keyFormulas.name: Kernel
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Kernel is the set of inputs that get sent to zero.

keyFormulas.name: One-to-one
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Only the zero input goes to zero.

commonMistakes: Putting \(T(e_1)\) and \(T(e_2)\) as rows instead of columns.
Thinking a map from \(\mathbb{R}^3\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\) could be one-to-one. It can't: at most 2 pivots for 3 columns.
Forgetting that linearity lets you break T(au+bv) into aT(u)+bT(v).
notationWarnings: Use T(e_1), T(e_2), not Te1, when writing transformation values.
Write \ker(T) for kernel and \operatorname{range}(T) for range.
When using a matrix, write T(x)=Ax to connect the function and the matrix.

problems.title: Build the standard matrix from basis vector images
problems.studentPromptLatex:
Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be linear with
\[T(e_1)=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad T(e_2)=\begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}.\]
Find the standard matrix for \(T\), compute \(T(5,-2)\), and decide whether \(T\) is one-to-one and onto.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: the columns are the images of the standard basis vectors. This is the main idea.

drawInstructions: Draw \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) in the input plane.
Draw their images \(T(e_1)\) and \(T(e_2)\) in the output plane.
Write the output vectors as columns of A.
Show that \(\det(A)=11\), so the map does not collapse area to zero.

walkthrough.label: Check one-to-one and onto
walkthrough.latex:
\[\det(A)=2(4)-3(-1)=11\neq 0.\]
So A is invertible. Since this is a map \(\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\), the transformation is both one-to-one and onto.

commonMistakes: Putting the two image vectors as rows.
Forgetting the determinant test only works this cleanly here because the matrix is square.
Saying onto because there are two outputs, instead of checking pivots/invertibility.

practiceLabPointer.note: More transformation and standard matrix practice.

problems.title: Kernel and range of a transformation
problems.studentPromptLatex:
Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be
\[T(x,y,z)=\begin{bmatrix}x-2y+z\\3x+y\end{bmatrix}.\]
Find the standard matrix, a basis for \(\ker(T)\), and the range of \(T\). Is \(T\) one-to-one? Is it onto?
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: kernel means set the output equal to zero. Range means look at pivot columns / output space.

drawInstructions: Draw a box labeled input R^3 and a box labeled output R^2.
Draw a line through the origin in R^3 labeled kernel direction (1,-3,-7).
Draw the whole output plane labeled range = R^2.
Say: a nonzero kernel means not one-to-one; full output plane means onto.

walkthrough.label: Find the kernel
walkthrough.latex:
Set \(T(x,y,z)=0\):
\[x-2y+z=0,\qquad 3x+y=0.\]
From the second equation, \(y=-3x\). Substitute into the first: \(x+6x+z=0\), so \(z=-7x\).

walkthrough.label: Find the range
walkthrough.latex: The two rows are independent, so the rank is 2. Since the output space is \(\mathbb{R}^2\), rank 2 means \(\operatorname{range}(T)=\mathbb{R}^2\).

walkthrough.label: Decide one-to-one and onto
walkthrough.latex: The kernel contains nonzero vectors, so \(T\) is not one-to-one. The range is all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), so \(T\) is onto.

problems.finalAnswerLatex: A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&1\\3&1&0\end{bmatrix},\quad \ker(T)=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-3,-7)\},\quad \operatorname{range}(T)=\mathbb{R}^2.\; T\text{ is onto but not one-to-one.}
commonMistakes: Setting the input equal to zero instead of the output when finding kernel.
Saying not onto just because the domain has three variables.
Forgetting that a nonzero kernel means not one-to-one.

practiceLabPointer.note: More practice with kernels, images, and transformation matrices.

problems.title: Using linearity with nonstandard input vectors
skills: Express a vector as a combination
Find transformation values from given data
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: we are not given \(T(e_1)\) directly. First write \((3,5)\) using the vectors we do know.

drawInstructions: Draw u=(1,2), v=(0,1), and target (3,5) in the input plane.
Draw the output as a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) only conceptually; exact 3D drawing is not necessary.

walkthrough.label: Write the target input as a combination
walkthrough.latex:
We want constants a and b with
\[a(1,2)+b(0,1)=(3,5).\]
From the first coordinate, \(a=3\). Then \(2a+b=5\), so \(6+b=5\), and \(b=-1\).

commonMistakes: Trying to plug (3,5) into a formula that was never given.
Forgetting the negative sign when using -T(0,1).
Assuming the given input vectors are \(e_1\) and \(e_2\). They are not.

practiceLabPointer.note: More practice with linearity and standard matrices.

wrapUpQuestions: What goes in the columns of a standard matrix?
What does a nonzero kernel tell us?
How can we use linearity when the input is written as a combination?

reviewSummary: Session 07 emphasizes columns-as-images and very simple kernel/range language. All computations were checked.

open.title: A matrix is a machine that moves space
say: Up to now a matrix has been a table of numbers. Today it becomes a function: vectors go in, vectors come out, and the whole plane gets stretched, sheared, or flipped.
The best part: to know everything the machine does, you only need to know where it sends e₁ and e₂.

ask.q: If I tell you where a linear map sends e₁ and e₂, can you tell me where it sends (5, −2)?

write: \(T(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=T(\mathbf u)+T(\mathbf v),\quad T(c\mathbf u)=cT(\mathbf u)\)

idea.title: Linear means straight lines stay straight and the origin stays put
say: A linear transformation respects adding and scaling. Geometrically: grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin doesn't move.
Because every vector is a combination of e₁ and e₂, knowing T(e₁) and T(e₂) pins down T completely. That's why those two outputs are the columns of the standard matrix.
Two questions we ask about every transformation: does anything besides 0 get crushed to 0 (the kernel), and which outputs can it hit (the range)?
draw: Draw a unit square with e₁ and e₂ on the left.
Draw a tilted parallelogram on the right, with the images T(e₁) and T(e₂) as its sides.
Write A = [T(e₁) T(e₂)] underneath with an arrow from each image to its column.

ask.q: Can a linear map send 0 to (1, 1)?
ask.a: No. T(0) = T(0 · v) = 0 · T(v) = 0 always.

ask.q: What does it mean if a nonzero vector is in the kernel?
ask.a: Two different inputs give the same output, so T isn't one-to-one.

launch.say: Build the matrix from T(e₁) and T(e₂), use it on (5, −2), and decide if T is one-to-one and onto.
circulate: Check that the images go in as columns, not rows.
Ask the first finisher why a nonzero determinant settles both questions here.

askFirst.q: Where do T(e₁) and T(e₂) go in the matrix?

steps.say: T(e₁) and T(e₂) go in as the columns of A.

ask.q: What is A times e₁ with this setup?
ask.a: Column 1, which is T(e₁). That's why columns work.

steps.why: A times eⱼ picks out column j. That's the whole reason the images become columns.

steps.say: Multiply: 5 times column 1 plus −2 times column 2 = (10 − 6, −5 − 8) = (4, −13).

ask.a: 5 copies of T(e₁) plus −2 copies of T(e₂).

steps.say: det A = 8 + 3 = 11. Nonzero, so A is invertible: T is one-to-one and onto.

ask.q: What does det A = 11 say about areas?
ask.a: T scales every area by 11 and doesn't flip orientation.

si07-p1.meaning: T turns the unit square into a parallelogram of area 11. Nothing gets crushed and every output is reachable, so every point of the plane has exactly one input.

ifStuck.if: a student writes the images as rows
ifStuck.then: multiply their matrix by e₁ and see if they get T(e₁).

si07-p1.transition: That map was square and invertible. Next: a map from 3D to 2D, which has to crush something.

launch.say: T goes from ℝ³ to ℝ². Find the matrix, the kernel, the range, and decide one-to-one and onto.
circulate: When finding the kernel, the output is set to 0, not the input.
Is anyone claiming it's not onto because the input has 3 variables? Push them to count pivots.

askFirst.q: Before computing: can a map from ℝ³ to ℝ² be one-to-one?
askFirst.a: No. At most 2 pivots for 3 columns, so there's always a free variable.

steps.say: Each output line gives one row of A: its coefficients of x, y and z.

ask.q: What size is A and why?

steps.say: Kernel: set the output to zero. From 3x + y = 0, y = −3x. Then x + 6x + z = 0 gives z = −7x.

ask.q: Why do we solve T(x) = 0 and not x = 0?
ask.a: The kernel is the set of inputs that produce the output 0.

steps.say: Let x = t: the kernel is all multiples of (1, −3, −7). A line through the origin.
The two rows are independent, so the rank is 2. The outputs fill all of ℝ².
Nonzero kernel: not one-to-one. Range is all of ℝ²: onto.

ask.q: Give two different inputs with the same output.

si07-p2.meaning: T squashes 3D space onto the 2D plane. A whole line of inputs, the multiples of (1, −3, −7), gets crushed to the origin, but every point of the output plane still gets hit.

ifStuck.if: a student says 'not onto because the domain is ℝ³'
ifStuck.then: ask what onto is about: the outputs. Check whether rank 2 reaches all of ℝ².

si07-p2.transition: Both problems so far gave us T(e₁), T(e₂) or a formula. The last one gives neither, only T of two other vectors.

launch.say: We know T on (1, 2) and (0, 1) only. Find T(3, 5).
circulate: Who is looking for a formula? There isn't one. Ask how (3, 5) relates to (1, 2) and (0, 1).

askFirst.q: What's the one property of T we're allowed to use?
askFirst.a: Linearity: T respects addition and scaling.

steps.say: Write (3, 5) as a(1, 2) + b(0, 1). The first coordinate forces a = 3, then 6 + b = 5 gives b = −1.

ask.q: Why is it easy to solve for a first?
ask.a: Only (1, 2) has a nonzero first entry.

steps.say: Linearity lets T pass through the combination: T(3, 5) = 3T(1, 2) − T(0, 1).

ask.q: Which two properties of linearity did we just use?

steps.why: Linearity means once you know T on a basis, you know it everywhere.

ask.q: Where do people drop a sign?

si07-p3.meaning: (1, 2) and (0, 1) form a basis of ℝ², so their images determine T completely, even though neither is e₁.

ifStuck.if: a student assumes (1, 2) and (0, 1) are e₁ and e₂
ifStuck.then: ask them to write e₁ = (1, 0) as a combination of the two given vectors.

wrap.write: Columns of A = T(e₁), T(e₂), … . Kernel = inputs sent to 0. Range = outputs hit. One-to-one ⟺ kernel = {0}.

exit.q: What goes in the columns of a standard matrix?
exit.a: The images of the standard basis vectors.

exit.q: What does a nonzero kernel tell you?
How do you find T(x) if you only know T on some other basis?
exit.a: Write x as a combination of that basis and use linearity.

wrap.next: Next session: determinants, the single number that measures how much a transformation scales area and whether it's invertible.
